body.markdown: At six in the morning, Riomaggiore wakes first. The bells of San Giovanni Battista ring out across the harbor, their deep bronze voice rolling down narrow lanes where laundry already hangs between shuttered windows. Five minutes later, Manarola answers—San Lorenzo's lighter, quicker tones echoing off the cliffside.

This is the conversation that shapes every day here. Not the tourist crowds or the train schedules, but this ancient call and response that threads through the five villages like the sentiero azzurro itself.

By seven, Corniglia joins from its hilltop perch—San Pietro's bells carry differently up there, floating down through vineyard terraces before reaching the sea. Vernazza's bells ring from Santa Margherita d'Antiochia, that pink-stoned church that guards the harbor, their sound mixing with the slap of fishing boats against the breakwater.

Monterosso, the eldest village, concludes the morning chorus. San Giovanni Battista's campanile—the tallest along this coast—sends its notes westward along the beach, where the last fishing nets are already being mended.

My grandmother used to say she could tell which church was ringing without looking up from her work. Each bell has its own personality, cast in different centuries by different hands. Some bright and insistent, others resonant and contemplative. Together they mark the hours: morning mass, noon, evening vespers, each village keeping time in its own rhythm while somehow staying synchronized.

Stand anywhere along the coastal path at sunset, and you'll hear them all. Five voices, five villages, one conversation that's been going on for centuries. The tourists photograph the colored houses, but locals like me—we listen for the bells. They tell us we're home.
